messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Fashion Designer
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 77

Here is a clinical vignette based on the patient you described.

---

It was a Tuesday morning in late September when the call came through. He was in the middle of a fitting for the spring collection, pinning a silk crepe bodice on a model who stood perfectly still. His phone buzzed on the cutting table. It was his wife’s number, but it was a stranger’s voice on the other end. The words—"your wife, a car, an intersection, the hospital"—landed like bolts of raw fabric, sharp and unprocessed. He left the model standing there, pins still in the dress, and ran.

He spent the next seventy-two hours in a vinyl chair in the surgical ICU waiting room. He remembers the smell of antiseptic and cold coffee, the way the fluorescent lights hummed a low, constant note. He remembers the surgeon’s face, careful and practiced, saying the words "traumatic brain injury" and "induced coma." He remembers holding her hand, which was cold and still, and watching the ventilator rise and fall. He has not been back to his studio since that Tuesday.

That was four months ago. His wife is home now, but she is not the same. She speaks more slowly, sometimes losing a word in the middle of a sentence. She has a tremor in her left hand and a deep, bone-tired fatigue that settles in by three in the afternoon. He is grateful she is alive. He tells himself this every morning. But the gratitude sits on top of something else, something darker that he cannot name.

He is a fashion designer. His world was built on precision, on the exact placement of a dart, the perfect fall of a hem, the mathematical grace of a bias cut. Now, he cannot look at a straight line without seeing the geometry of the intersection where it happened. He cannot hear the sound of a zipper without flinching, because it sounds too much like the rhythmic hiss of the ventilator. He tried, once, to sketch a new silhouette. He picked up a charcoal pencil, and his hand began to shake. The line he drew was jagged, broken, a seismic readout of a heart attack. He threw the sketchbook across the room.

He is a man who lives in a state of constant, low-grade electrical storm. He cannot sit still, but he cannot move forward. He paces the apartment at night, checking the locks on the doors three, four, five times. He calls his wife’s phone from the next room, just to hear it ring, just to be sure she is still there. He has started to avoid the kitchen, because that is where he replays the phone call—the sound of the stranger’s voice, the way the world tilted, the feeling of his own pulse in his throat. He cannot drive past the hospital. He takes three different routes to the grocery store, all of them longer, to avoid the sight of the glass-and-steel building.

His wife asks him to sit with her, to watch a movie, to talk. He tries. He sits next to her on the couch, but his body is rigid, his mind scanning the room for threats. He hears the soft thud of a car door closing outside and his heart seizes. He sees a news report about a car accident and he has to leave the room, his breath shallow, his vision tunneling. He feels a deep, volcanic guilt for his own agitation. She is the one who was hurt. She is the one who needs care. And he is the one falling apart.

He told me last session that he feels like he is still in that vinyl chair in the ICU. That time has stopped. That he is waiting for a doctor to come through a door that never opens. He is a designer of beautiful, functional things, and now he cannot design a way out of this. He is a man who built a life on the elegance of a line, and his life has become a jagged, unfinished sketch.
